body: Bitcoin ETF demand returned last week, then faded. Now price is testing the ETF buyers' cost basis Money came back into US spot bitcoin exchange-traded funds last week, but it didn't stay. The funds took in about $1.07 billion over the first three sessions, then lost $773.5 million over the final two, according to preliminary Farside data. That left a provisional net inflow of $301.2 million for the week to October 23. title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6691 – Reuters estimate
body: The People's Bank of China is due to set the daily USD/CNY reference rate at around 0115 GMT (2115 US Eastern time), a fixing that remains one of the most closely watched signals in Asian foreign exchange markets. China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility. Intervention can take the form of direct buying or selling of yuan, adjustments to liquidity conditions, or guidance through state-owned banks. As a result, the daily fixing is often interpreted as a policy signal rather than just a technical reference point.

title: UK autumn budget preview: Can Healey calm markets and change BOE rate hike bets?
body: The UK autumn budget is coming up on 28 October, just a week before the BOE's next monetary policy decision. And with inflation concerns still hanging over the economy, the government's fiscal plans could have a say in how interest rate expectations develop over the coming months. For now, traders are pricing in roughly 99% odds of a 25 bps rate hike at the November meeting next week. So unless something really unexpected happens, that decision looks pretty much settled. As for December though, that is another story. Traders are currently pricing in around 47% odds of another rate hike before the year is out. That's essentially a coin toss and the autumn budget could be one to help tip expectations one way or the other. So, what should traders be looking out for? For starters, the general expectation is for a fairly cautious budget - one with modest tax increases and targeted support for households rather than any major spending commitments. The backdrop is one where the government's fiscal headroom is looking rather uncomfortable. According to EY, that buffer against the government's fiscal rules has shrunk from £23.6 billion in March to an estimated £11.3 billion. That is largely because of higher borrowing costs and the economic fallout from the Iran conflict. The latest Reuters survey suggests that Healey should try and rebuild that buffer to around £15-16 billion to reassure bond investors. So, that at least gives us some useful benchmark for judging the budget.

title: What is the FOMC blackout period and why do central banks have one
body: Central banks influence financial markets through both interest rate decisions and communication. Speeches and interviews can change expectations for future monetary policy, affecting bonds, currencies, equities and so on. To limit these signals immediately before policy decisions, many central banks have a blackout period. A blackout period is a predefined period during which policymakers are restricted from publicly discussing monetary policy or the upcoming decision. The rules vary across central banks, but the purpose is to ensure that official announcements remain the primary source of information about the committee's decision. The Federal Reserve's FOMC blackout period begins at midnight eastern time on the second Saturday before a scheduled meeting and ends at 11:59 p.m. on the day after the meeting. Other central banks follow similar practices. The ECB observes a quiet period beginning seven days before a monetary policy meeting. The Bank of England restricts Monetary Policy Committee members' communications for 8-9 days before the official rate announcement. The Bank of Canada restricts communications on monetary policy and the economic outlook during the week before the rate decision. Before the blackout, policymakers' speeches can provide clues about their views on inflation, growth and upcoming interest rate decisions.

title: Stock earnings pick of the week: Can Microsoft's AI growth still justify its spending spree?
body: Microsoft will report earnings on Wednesday, 28 October, and once again this will be one of those times where the numbers themselves might not be the biggest story. Now, don't get me wrong. The results will still matter. Analysts are expecting revenue of around $90.6 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, alongside EPS of $4.71. Those are strong growth numbers, especially when you consider just how big Microsoft already is. But as has been the case with most big tech earnings, investors will be paying much closer attention to what management has to say about Microsoft's AI ambitions more than anything else. And that will particularly be the case after the recent selloff in tech stocks over the past two weeks. Microsoft is already spending an extraordinary amount of money to build out its AI infrastructure. The firm's capital expenditure, including finance leases, hit roughly $41 billion in the previous quarter and management expects that figure to exceed $50 billion this quarter. Just think about that for a moment. We're talking about more than $50 billion in spending over three months alone. Of course, Microsoft has good reasons to be investing so aggressively. Azure revenue grew 43% year-on-year in the previous quarter, with management guiding for roughly 45% growth in constant currency this quarter. Besides, the underlying backdrop signals that demand remains strong enough that available computing capacity is still struggling to keep up.

The $4,000 level is still holding for now, with price hovering around $4,007. So, I wouldn't go as far as calling this a confirmed technical breakdown just yet. title: Heads up: European daylight saving time has ended, here's what traders need to know
body: This is just a quick heads up for traders before we get too far into the new trading week. If you're wondering why European markets seem to be opening a little later than usual today, well it is because we're back to that time of the year again. Daylight saving time ended across most of Europe over the weekend, with clocks moving back one hour on Sunday, 25 October. That means the UK is now back on GMT time, while much of continental Europe has switched to CET time. For those of you trading from outside Europe, particularly in Asia, this means European market openings and economic data releases will now arrive one hour later on your local clock. For example, the London stock market will now open at 16:00 in Singapore and Hong Kong instead of 15:00 previously. But here's the other little wrinkle to keep in mind. The US hasn't made the switch just yet. US clocks will only move back on Sunday, 1 November. So for this week at least, the time difference between London and New York is temporarily four hours instead of the usual five hours. That also means a longer overlap between London and New York trading sessions this week, something worth keeping in mind for those watching forex liquidity around the US market open. Anyway, there's nothing particularly dramatic here. It is just one of those small calendar changes that can easily catch traders off guard.
